title: Running Seasonal Sale Pages? Here’s How to Optimize Them for Search
content:
Do you run an online store and plan seasonal sales such as White Friday or year-end discounts? Whether you create a new page every season or reuse your old sale pages, it pays to know the right way to set them up for search engines.

That approach comes down to two decisions. First, keep each occasion’s sale page on a single URL that does not change from one year to the next; this is an explicit Google recommendation. Second, put the sale price and sale dates on the product pages themselves, not on the seasonal page, and include the time and time zone with every date.

When you publish the page, and how you write the sale dates, both affect what your customers find when they search for your deals. A sale page published only a few days before the season may not be added to Google’s search index before the season starts, so it will not appear in search results for people looking for your offers. And if you submit your products to Merchant Center, the Google tool where stores send their product data for use in Google Search, Shopping and other Google services, your sale there may start and end later than you intended if you write its dates without a time zone.

The sections below answer your practical questions in order: whether to create a new page for each season, how to prepare it, where to put the sale price and dates, and how to check that your store is ready before the season begins.

This guide is for store owners and marketers on any platform, and it covers only Google’s unpaid search results and product data in Merchant Center. Keep in mind from the start that Google does not guarantee how a sale price will appear in results in any country, and that results vary with factors including the searcher’s location. The steps below make your data correct and eligible to appear; they do not force any particular display. The code-level details are in an optional section for developers at the end of the guide.

Should I Create a New Page for Every Season?

The first thing to decide before any season is the URL of your sale page, and Google’s recommendation is clear: do not create a page with a new URL every season; reuse one URL for the same occasion every time.

In October 2020, Google published an article on best practices for sale seasons, recommending that a recurring sale event have a recurring URL rather than a new URL each time it runs. Its example was the path /sale/black-friday instead of /sale/2020/black-friday. Then, in July 2021, an article on deals best practices repeated the advice to reuse the same URL every year.

Say your store sells abayas and you have a White Friday sale page. Under this recommendation, the page stays on the same URL every year and you update its content when the season comes back, instead of creating a new page each year with the year in its URL.

The 2020 article gave no reason for this recommendation and did not tie it to any search feature. But it makes sense alongside the article’s other recommendation: publish the page early so Google can discover and index it, that is, add it to the pages that can appear in its search results. A recurring URL is one page that is discovered and indexed once; a new URL is a new page waiting to be discovered and indexed every season. This is our reading of the recommendation, not a reason the article states.

The same logic applies to Hijri-calendar seasons: do not put the Hijri year in your Ramadan page URL, for example by adding 1448 to it. That URL would change next season, just like one carrying a Gregorian year. This is our application of Google’s recommendation to Hijri seasons, not something Google says; neither of its two articles covers the Hijri calendar.

Putting the year in the page title, on the other hand, is your call, not a Google recommendation for Arab markets: include it if you think it is clearer for visitors, as long as the URL itself stays year-free.

How Do I Prepare the Seasonal Page Before and After the Sale?

Once you have chosen a fixed URL for the page, you still need to decide when to publish it, what to put on it and what to do with it when the sale ends.

When should I publish it?

Publish the seasonal page well before the season starts. In its 2020 article, Google recommended creating the page early so it can discover and index it before the season, and making sure it is not blocked from crawling, meaning your site settings do not stop Google from visiting and reading it. It also recommended linking to the page from your homepage to signal its importance.

There is a practical reason to start early: crawling, meaning Google visiting and reading the page, can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks, according to Google’s documentation on asking Google to recrawl. A page published only a few days before the season may not be indexed by the time it starts.

If your store is preparing for Ramadan or Eid, work out when to publish and link the page from that year’s season date, not from a fixed Gregorian date. Ramadan and the two Eids follow the Hijri calendar and do not fall on the same Gregorian date from one year to the next.

What should I put on it?

When you publish the page, include what makes its topic clear to both Google and visitors. The points below come from Google’s 2021 article, which was written to help stores appear in the deals carousel. The article said this feature was then limited to the United States, and the Google pages this guide relies on do not mention it being available in any Arab country. Nor does the article say these points improve visibility in Arab countries, but they make the page understandable to Google and visitors alike:

  • Visible text on the page that names and describes the occasion. The article justifies this point on grounds unrelated to the carousel: such text may help Google understand that the page is about a specific sale.
  • The text on your banner images repeated in the page copy and in the images’ alt text, the text description attached to each image, so the offer does not live only inside an image.
  • General information published in advance if the details are only revealed on the day of the event. Once you update the page with the details, ask Google to recrawl it. A crawl request does not guarantee inclusion, though, and repeating the request does not speed it up.

What should I do with it when the sale ends?

When the season’s sale ends, keep the page live on its URL and update its content. Neither of Google’s two articles covers what to do with the page between seasons, so the following is a recommendation that follows from their advice on recurring URLs:

  • State clearly on the page that this season’s offers have ended, and what visitors can find there now.
  • Remove expired prices and countdown timers; they mislead visitors.
  • Do not delete the page and recreate it, and do not redirect it to a different URL every year; update it in place next season.

The same rule applies if your store’s seasonal page is a category, a product collection or a platform page: reuse it every season instead of creating a new one.

Where Do I Put the Sale Price and Sale Dates?

The seasonal page introduces the occasion and brings the offers together; the sale price and sale dates belong on the page of each discounted product.

You can provide your product data, including price and sale dates, to Google Search in two ways that Google documents. The first is structured data: markup inside the product page that describes the product in a language search engines can read, including its name, price and sale dates. The second is Merchant Center. You do not have to use Merchant Center; you can choose either method or combine them, and Google says combining them increases a product’s eligibility for different search experiences.

As for why the product page, the answer is in Google’s merchant listing guide, the guide to merchant listing markup. It explains that this markup is meant for pages where a shopper can buy the product, and Google recommends placing it on product pages rather than on pages that list products or show a category. The seasonal page is the second kind, so the price and its dates belong on each product page.

How does Google know a product is on sale?

It is enough for the product’s structured data to carry two prices: the current price as usual, and the original pre-sale price marked as a strikethrough price, which Google’s documentation calls the “strikethrough price”. The current price then automatically becomes a sale price, according to Google’s documentation.

An illustrative example: an abaya priced at SAR 240 that you mark down to SAR 180 for the season. The current price in its data is 180, and the strikethrough original price is 240.

If the problem lies in the prices and data of your whole catalog rather than a single product, that is a job for product data organization before it is a markup job.

How do I write the sale dates?

After the price, specify in the product page’s structured data when the sale starts and when it ends. In its merchant listing guide, Google recommends writing the start and end dates together so the sale is clearly defined, and adding the time and time zone to each date. The time zone here is your city’s offset from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), such as +03:00 for Riyadh. The start must not come after the end.

So if your sale starts at midnight Riyadh time, write the day, the hour and the UTC offset together, not the day alone.

If your platform writes this data for you, the section “How do I check that my store is ready?” below shows how to verify what it outputs.

Why Might My Sale Start Late in Merchant Center?

If you submit your products to Merchant Center, enter the sale dates there too, and watch out for a rule that can delay your sale.

Merchant Center has an optional attribute for sale dates that combines the start and end in a single value, and it only works together with the sale price attribute; its name and format are in the technical section. The Merchant Center help page for this attribute documents two rules: if the time is missing, the sale starts at 00:00 on the start date and ends at 23:59 on the end date; and if the time zone is missing, the value is interpreted as UTC.

The second rule directly affects when your sale runs in Merchant Center. If you enter the dates in Merchant Center without a time zone and your store’s time zone is ahead of UTC, the sale period Merchant Center applies to your product data starts later than you intended, and ends later too. The delay equals your store’s offset from UTC on the sale days themselves.

Say your abaya store is in Riyadh, which is on UTC+03:00, you want your White Friday sale to start at midnight, and you enter the dates in Merchant Center without a time zone. Google then reads the start in Merchant Center as midnight UTC, which is 3:00 a.m. in Riyadh. The start in Merchant Center is delayed by three hours, and so is the end.

An illustrative example with three cities (not an exhaustive list), for a date entered in Merchant Center without a time zone:

Egypt is a special case: its UTC offset changes between summer and winter, and Ramadan or Eid can fall in either period, so calculate the offset for the actual sale dates, not for today’s date. If your store is in another city, calculate the delay using your city’s offset from UTC on your sale days.

This delay affects the sale period Merchant Center applies to the product data Google uses. The sale in your own store starts and ends according to your platform settings and is not affected by what you entered in Merchant Center.

This UTC rule is specific to Merchant Center. For structured data on the product page, the merchant listing guide does not say which time zone is assumed for a date without one, and neither do Google’s pages on product markup and structured data policies. The guide simply recommends including the time zone. So do not assume it is UTC or your store’s time zone; write the UTC offset explicitly in both your structured data and Merchant Center.

What Mistakes Should I Avoid?

Before you check your store, review these five mistakes on the seasonal page and product pages:

  1. Product or sale structured data on the seasonal page. Do not add product or price offer structured data to the seasonal page, or “Event” or “Sale” structured data in the hope of a special feature; the documentation that covers sale prices and dates ties them to the product page.
  2. A price or discount in the structured data that visitors cannot see. Your structured data must match what is on the page, so do not include a price or discount that visitors cannot see.
  3. A past expiry date on an offer that is still live. Google’s documentation says a product listing may not appear if the price expiry date in the structured data is in the past; the property’s name is in the technical section. And do not copy dates from documentation examples as they are, because some of them are already in the past.
  4. Structured data generated with JavaScript. Google recommends placing product structured data in the page’s initial HTML, that is, the page as your store’s server sends it before any scripts run. It notes that JavaScript-generated structured data can make Shopping crawls less frequent and less reliable for fast-changing prices and availability.
  5. Expecting the price to appear in a particular way. Structured data makes a product eligible; it does not guarantee how it is displayed.

How Do I Check That My Store Is Ready?

Everything above assumes your product pages output the sale and its dates the way you want, so verify that before the season. If your structured data comes from your platform, theme or a plugin, what Google reads is what that tool writes into the page, not what you entered in your dashboard.

What does my store platform output?

Start with what your platform outputs or documents. Here is what the sources of three platforms show:

WooCommerce. The latest WooCommerce release at the time of writing is 11.2.1. In this version, the core structured data code writes the sale end date as a date only, with no time or time zone, and does not write a start date. This applies both to a simple product on sale and to a variable product whose options have different prices, such as an abaya priced by size. The merchant listing guide does not say how Google interprets an end date without a time; what it does say is that you should include the time and time zone. A date alone leaves the exact moment the sale ends open to interpretation. SEO plugins or themes may also replace this markup with their own, so the reference point is what your own page outputs.

Salla. Salla’s help page on importing product quantities and prices says the import updates the sale price and the “sale end date”. It also says product options do not take a separate end date but follow the offer end date for the product as a whole. The page does not mention a start date or cover structured data, and at the time of writing Salla files it under “Old articles”. So this page does not document what a Salla store writes in the structured data for a discounted product; check it in your own store.

Shopify. Shopify’s Help Center describes setting up a sale by entering a “Compare-at price” higher than the current price on the product page in the admin. The help page does not cover structured data, so check what your theme outputs.

How do I check a product page?

Whatever your platform, whether one of these three, Zid, another platform or a custom-built store, run these steps on a product page in your store:

  1. Open a product with a sale that is live right now. If the sale is scheduled and has not started yet, check again once it starts; the sale data may not be written into the page before then.
  2. Enter the page URL in the Rich Results Test. Rich results are search results that show extra information about a page, such as the price. According to its documentation, the test shows the rich result types it found on the page, along with any errors or suggestions.
  3. Review the values yourself: the sale price, the strikethrough original price, the start and end dates, and whether each date carries a time and the correct UTC offset. The test’s documentation does not say it validates dates or time zones, or that it shows how the result will look in a particular country.
  4. If your site is added to Search Console, the Google tool for monitoring how your site appears in search, inspect the URL with the URL Inspection tool. Then run a live test (Test live URL) to see a screenshot of the page as Google fetches it, plus information about it, according to the URL Inspection tool help page.
  5. Monitor the Merchant listings report in Search Console once Google has crawled your product pages.

If the structured data shows up in the test but your developer cannot find it when searching the page source (the method is in the technical section), it is most likely generated with JavaScript, which is the fourth mistake in the list above. And if it turns out your store does not output sale dates at all, you have three options: your platform’s own settings, an app or plugin that writes structured data, or the sale dates attribute in Merchant Center if you submit your products there.

Does This Guarantee My Sale Price Will Show in Google?

Even if your store gets everything right, Google does not guarantee it will show these features in any country, Arab or otherwise. In its structured data policies, Google says structured data makes a feature possible but does not guarantee it will appear, even if the markup is correct, and that it tailors results based on many variables, including search history and the searcher’s location. Its product markup documentation adds that Google does not guarantee a price drop will be shown.

What Merchant Center offers also varies by country: the Merchant Center help page on supported countries lists the countries you can target with Shopping ads and free listings, and where the Shopping tab is available, so check it for your country before the season. But a country being targetable in Merchant Center does not mean a strikethrough price or a particular display format will appear in its search results; that page does not cover how prices are shown in search at all. So do not build your plan on your sale price appearing in Google in a particular way in any market.

For measurement, Search Console gives you the Merchant listings report and the Performance report. Because your seasonal page URL is fixed, you can compare its performance in the Performance report from one season to the next on the same URL, for example this year’s White Friday page against last year’s. That is a practical measurement benefit of a fixed URL, not a promise of better rankings.

If what you need is a review of your store’s visibility across search as a whole, not just the seasonal page, that is the core of e-commerce SEO.

What Should I Do Before and After the Season?

Here are the guide’s steps in timeline order, so you can come back to them before every season:

  1. Weeks before the season: publish the seasonal page on its fixed URL, not blocked from crawling and linked from the homepage, and check a discounted product page using the steps above.
  2. In the same period: make sure your site can handle seasonal traffic. The Merchant Center checklist for preparing for events recommends this, noting that products may be disapproved in Merchant Center if the site goes down or times out.
  3. 3 to 5 business days before the event, and no earlier than 30 days before it: submit your new product data to Merchant Center, if you use it, according to the Merchant Center checklist for preparing for events.
  4. At least 24 hours before the promotion starts: submit your promotions to Merchant Center, if they are available in your account, according to the same checklist, which notes that review is usually completed within 24 hours of the promotion’s start date but can take up to 72 hours.
  5. Just before the event: do not move the price elements on the product page, and do not switch to showing the price or discount with JavaScript or animation; according to the same checklist, this can cause temporary product disapprovals in Merchant Center.
  6. On launch day: check the UTC offset in your structured data and in Merchant Center, and request a recrawl if the details were revealed late.
  7. After the season: make sure the sales and their dates have ended on your products and that no live offer carries a past price expiry date, then update the seasonal page, or the same category or collection, in place.

If your seasonal page is not indexed in time, the problem is one of discovery and indexing, not of your offers; see why your website is not showing in search.

For Developers: Technical Details (Optional)

This section is for anyone who writes product markup themselves or reviews what their platform outputs. Store owners do not need it to apply the steps above, but it brings together the property names, code examples and a detailed look at what WooCommerce outputs.

The strikethrough price in product markup

Google recognizes three types of price in product markup: the active price (the current price), the strikethrough original price and the member price. For Google to understand that a product is on sale, it is enough to write the current price as the offer price as usual, then add a second price, the original price, marked with the priceType property set to StrikethroughPrice. The active price then automatically becomes a sale price, according to Google’s documentation. Google accepts the value ListPrice instead for a transition period, and asks that you do not put priceType on the active price itself.

Sale dates in structured data: validFrom, validThrough and priceValidUntil

The validFrom property sets the moment the offer price takes effect, and validThrough or priceValidUntil sets the moment it ends. In July 2026, Google added a section on sale price duration to its merchant listing guide explaining how to write them. Here is a summary:

  • The start uses the validFrom property, and the end uses validThrough or priceValidUntil, both in ISO 8601 format.
  • Write the start and end together so the sale is clearly defined; the start must not come after the end.
  • Add the time and time zone. The documentation recommends including the time and time zone in ISO 8601 format to ensure accuracy in Google’s systems.

Where do the properties go? In one of two places:

  • On the Offer node itself, if the price it carries (price) is the active sale price.
  • Or on the PriceSpecification node for the sale price. In this position priceValidUntil is not valid, so use validThrough.

Which property for the end? Google accepts both properties on Offer, and one of its examples uses priceValidUntil with a date and time. But if the exact end time matters to you, validThrough is the clearer choice: the schema.org specification defines it as accepting a date or a date-time, whereas it defines priceValidUntil as a date. validThrough also works in both positions. This is a practical recommendation, not a Google rule.

An illustrative example of a discounted product in a store on UTC+03:00 (the product, prices and URL are hypothetical):

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org/",
  "@type": "Product",
  "name": "Illustrative example: Linen abaya",
  "offers": {
    "@type": "Offer",
    "url": "https://example.com/products/linen-abaya",
    "price": 180.00,
    "priceCurrency": "SAR",
    "validFrom": "2027-07-08T00:00:00+03:00",
    "validThrough": "2027-07-11T23:59:59+03:00",
    "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock",
    "priceSpecification": {
      "@type": "UnitPriceSpecification",
      "priceType": "https://schema.org/StrikethroughPrice",
      "price": 240.00,
      "priceCurrency": "SAR"
    }
  }
}

In this example, the sale price (SAR 180) starts at 00:00 on July 8 (UTC+03:00) and ends in the last minute of July 11, and the strikethrough original price is SAR 240. If you used priceValidUntil instead of validThrough with the same value, the example would still be valid on Offer. The dates here are for illustration only: replace them with your own sale start and end dates, and never leave a past end date on an offer that is still live.

The priceValidUntil property is the one meant in the third mistake on the list of mistakes: Google’s documentation says a product listing may not appear if its value is a date in the past.

The example covers only the offer and price. A real product page needs other properties that the merchant listing guide requires, such as a product image, so refer to the guide when implementing. After you edit the values in the code, and before you add it to your page, you can paste it into the Rich Results Test by choosing “Code” instead of a URL, as the Rich Results Test help page explains.

If you are checking a published page manually, search its source for a <script type="application/ld+json"> block, then for a second price marked with StrikethroughPrice (or ListPrice), for validFrom, and for validThrough or priceValidUntil.

The sale_price_effective_date format in Merchant Center

The sale_price_effective_date attribute sets the period during which the sale price is shown, and it only works together with the sale price attribute sale_price. Here are the rules for writing it, according to the Merchant Center help page for this attribute:

  • Start and end in a single value, separated by a / character.
  • Each end is a date, time and UTC offset, in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm followed by the offset without a colon (+0300), or the letter Z for UTC.
  • Length: 51 characters at most.

An illustrative example for the same period as in the structured data example:

2027-07-08T00:00+0300/2027-07-11T23:59+0300

The value is 43 characters long, within the limit. The same rule as in the previous example applies: use your own sale dates, and never leave an expired date on a live offer.

The difference between the two formats in short: structured data writes the UTC offset with a colon (+03:00) and across two properties, while Merchant Center writes it without a colon and in a single value.

What WooCommerce 11.2.1 outputs, in detail

For a simple product on sale, the core code writes the sale price inside UnitPriceSpecification, along with validThrough set to the sale end date as a date only (in the form 2027-07-11, for example), and puts the same date in priceValidUntil. If the sale has no end date, it puts December 31 of the following year in priceValidUntil. It does not write validFrom, and it marks the regular price with the value ListPrice.

For a variable product whose options have different prices, the same code writes an aggregate offer (AggregateOffer) with the lowest and highest prices, and marks the sale price in it with the value SalePrice, with no regular price marked as ListPrice. The same date notes apply to both types: the end is a date only, and there is no validFrom.

seo.rank_math_description: Reuse one URL for your seasonal sale page every season and add a time zone to sale dates, especially in Merchant Center, which assumes UTC without one.
